query: I am interested in high-entropy alloys for extreme temperature applications. How can we predict melting properties such as the melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity for multi-component systems where experimental data is sparse or unreliable due to high melting points? I am looking for a hypothesis on a computational methodology that balances accuracy with the need to screen vast compositional spaces, along with prior evidence on why standard approaches struggle in this regime and what a valid boundary condition for such a method would be.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid computational screening methodology combining CALPHAD thermodynamic modeling with a machine-learned surrogate for lattice distortion energy can accurately predict melting temperatures and entropy of fusion for refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) in compositional spaces where experimental data is sparse, by explicitly accounting for severe local lattice distortion as the primary structural mediator of thermal stability.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-principal-element alloy system (≥5 elements) comprising refractory metals (e.g., W, Mo, Ta, Nb, V) with severe local lattice distortion due to atomic size mismatch, existing as a body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution or a BCC+B2 two-phase system.
generation.intervention: Implement a computational workflow that first uses CALPHAD to identify stable phase regions and then applies a machine-learned surrogate model trained on known lattice distortion metrics to predict the enthalpy of fusion and melting temperature, bypassing the need for expensive first-principles calculations for every composition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature regime (elevated temperatures > 1000 K) and vast compositional spaces (quinary or higher order systems) where standard first-principles methods are computationally prohibitive due to the scaling of calculation time with the number of components.
generation.structural_mediator: Severe local lattice distortion caused by the deviation of atoms from ideal lattice sites due to the presence of multiple elements with different atomic sizes, which impedes dislocation motion and alters thermodynamic stability.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion in RHEAs stabilize the solid solution phase against melting; the proposed method leverages the correlation between lattice distortion magnitude and the energy barrier for phase transition (melting) to predict melting properties without simulating the full liquid state dynamics for every composition.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid method will successfully screen vast compositional spaces to identify RHEA compositions with melting temperatures and entropy of fusion values within 5% of experimental benchmarks (where available) or consistent with theoretical limits, while reducing computational time from thousands of hours to a few hours per system, overcoming the scaling limitations of pure CALPHAD or DFT approaches.
generation.baseline: Standard CALPHAD calculations alone, which require massive computational time for high-order systems (e.g., quinary systems with 1 at.% step size taking thousands of hours) and often struggle to accurately predict melting properties in systems with severe lattice distortion without extensive experimental database inputs.
generation.boundary: The method is valid for single-phase BCC solid solutions or BCC+B2 systems with refractory elements; it may fail for systems with complex intermetallic precipitation or non-equilibrium phases not captured by the training data of the surrogate model.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding the accuracy of the machine-learned surrogate model when applied to compositional spaces significantly outside the training set (e.g., novel element combinations not previously studied for lattice distortion effects), and the potential for non-equilibrium processing effects (e.g., additive manufacturing) to alter the predicted melting behavior compared to equilibrium thermodynamics.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a quinary refractory HEA system (e.g., W-Mo-Ta-Nb-V) with a known experimental melting point. Run the proposed hybrid workflow to predict the melting temperature and entropy of fusion. Compare the predictions against the experimental values obtained via differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) or high-temperature optical pyrometry.
measurements: Predicted melting temperature (Tm) from hybrid model
Predicted entropy of fusion (ΔSfus) from hybrid model
Experimental entropy of fusion (ΔSfus) from DSC
Computational time required for the hybrid workflow vs. pure CALPHAD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the predicted melting temperature deviates by more than 10% from the experimental value for any composition in the quinary system, or if the computational time reduction is less than 90% compared to the pure CALPHAD approach for the same system.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations. The fields of aerospace and fossil energy have benefited from decades of the development of Ni-base superalloys. However, to obtain further efficiency gains and environmental friendliness, developing new materials with inexpensive, light, and strong characteristics is required. Numerous efforts can be found in the development of novel ferritic superalloys containing a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix with ordered B2 and/or L2 1 precipitates due to their good creep resistance at elevated temperatures and relatively lower densities [1] , [2] . However, these emerging precipitation-strengthened ferritic alloys still face some drawbacks, such as the low high-temperature strength and not lightweight, which limit their applications. To overcome these issues, new alloy-design strategies are required. Recently, the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) has revolutionized the traditional alloy-design strategy, using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components [3] – [10] . The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
